title: A rock-inscription at Tandalam
html:
A ROCK-INSCRIPTION AT TANDALAM.

By E. HULTZSCH, PH.D.

The existence of this inscription (No. 1 of 1892) was brought to my notice by Mr. E. Srinivasachari, Deputy Collector, Madras. It is engraved on a rock near the tank at Taṇḍalam, a village in the Kārvėtinagar Zamîndârî, 4½ miles west by north of Arkôṇam Junction. With the exception of the two Grantha words svasti śrî in the beginning, the alphabet is Tamiĵ, and resembles that of the Vêlûr rock-inscription of Kaṇṇaradêva.4

The inscription is dated in the 10th year of Śatti, the king of the Kâḍavas, i.e. Pallavas.5 It consists of two Tamiĵ verses, each of which states that Pallavamahârâja built a sluice for the tank at Taṇḍalam. The donor may have been either a relative of, or identical with, Śatti, who, as his title implies, claimed descent from the ancient Pallava dynasty. Pôliyûr-nâḍu, to which Taṇḍalam belonged, was perhaps named after the present Pôlûr, a village 3 miles north-north-west of Arkôṇam Junction.

The Veûkaṭêśa-Perumâl temple on the Tirupati hill bears on the north wall of its first prâkâra four Chôla inscriptions, which were copied from their (now lost) originals when the temple was rebuilt in the fortieth year of Vîra-Nârasimhadêva-Yâdavarâya. The second and third of these four copies (Nos. 62 and 63 of 1888-89) are dated in the 14th year of “Paratrama-hêndravarman” and “Paratravarman”— evidently misreadings of the copyist for Parakêsarivarman. These two inscriptions record gifts by Śâmavai alias Kâḍavaṇ-Perundêvi, the daughter of Pallava-Perkaḍaiyâr,6 (and) the queen of Śattiviḍaṅgaṇ alias Śrî-Kâḍapatṭigaĵ.7 It is not improbable that this Pallava king Śattiviḍaṅgaṇ (i.e. Śakti-Viṭaṅka),8 who was a contemporary of the early Chôla king Parakêsarivarman,9 is the same person as the Pallava king Śatti (i.e. Śakti). In this case the subjoined inscription would belong roughly to the second half of the ninth century of the Christian era.

aindil=iduvittâ=ñi(ñi)-
2 điya-śi(śi)r Pa[l*]lavamârâyañ paśi ni(nî)kki Tanđalattu=kkall-ivar
ni(nî)r-êri-kkaliñgum=anđattu-
3 [l]ôr madippavañ [|| 1*] Pôli[yu(yû)]r-nâttu=Ttanđalatt=êri-kka-
4 ling=amaittâñn=oñ-Damil-ppâr-mañgai-dâñ
5 virumbum Pallavamârâyañ=eîr-pu(pû)-mañgai-da[n]=
6 gôñ purindu [|| 2*][ø-]

TRANSLATION.

Hail! Prosperity! (Verse 1.) In (the year) twice five (i.e. ten), which was engraved on palm-leaves,12 (from) the year when (the name of) Šatti, the king of the Kádavas, was entered on a gold leaf,13— Pallavamârâyañ of enduring fame, who is respected by (all) the inhabitants of the world, having freed (the villagers) of hunger, caused to be built also a sluice, composed of stones, for the water-tank at Tanđalam.

(V. 2.) The lord of the beautiful goddess of the (lotus) flower (i.e. Lakshmî), Pallavamârâyañ, who is beloved by the excellent goddess of the Tamiî country, graciously constructed a sluice for the tank at Tanđalam in Pôliyûr-nâdu.

Footnotes

1(p. 25, n. 1) From two inked estampages. 2(p. 25, n. 2) Read Chiraiyûr. 3(p. 25, n. 3) Literally, ‘while Bāṇarāja cut (him) down.’

4↩(p. 25, n. 4) Above, Vol. IV. No. 9. 5↩(p. 25, n. 5) See above, p. 23 f.

6↩(p. 25, n. 6) Perkaḍai seems to be a Tamiĵ form of the Kanarese pergade and the Telugu preygada, ‘a minister.’

7↩(p. 25, n. 7) Compare Mr. Venkayya’s paper in the Madras Christian College Magazine for August 1890. Kâḍapatṭi seems to be a mistake of the copyist for Kâḍupatṭi, which occurs in a Pallava inscription at Conjeeveram (loc. cit.) and in two Gaṅga-Pallava inscriptions (South-Ind. Inscr. Vol. III. p. 92 f.). Compare also Kâḍuvatṭi (above, Vol. V. p. 171 and note 1) and Kâḍuvitṭêsvara (ibid. p. 143).

8↩(p. 25, n. 8) Dantiśakti-Viṭaṅkî alias Lôkamahâdêvî, a queen of the Chôla king Râjarâja I., built a shrine in the Pañchanadêsvara temple at Tiruvaiyâru; see my Annual Report for 1894-95, p. 4.

9↩(p. 25, n. 9) See above, Vol. V. p. 42 and note 7.

10↩(p. 26, n. 1) From an inked stampage.

11↩(p. 26, n. 2) In this verse "đ=êđ=iya" rhymes with ntdiya and Tanđa° with "m=ayđa".

12↩(p. 26, n. 3) I.e. with which all documents issued at this time had to begin.

13↩(p. 26, n. 4) This seems to refer to some custom observed at the coronation of a king; compare South-Ind. Inscr. Vol. III. p 185 and note 2.
